HEARD:  January 9-13, 2006; January 16-18, 2006

CROLL  J.

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

[
1
]

This case
is about A.J.K., a 6-year-old girl.  A.J.K.’s mother seeks permanent custody of
A.J.K., and permission to move to Japan with her; however, she seeks custody
regardless of whether she is permitted to move to Japan.  A.J.K.’s father
resists the mother’s custody application, and seeks custody himself.

Background facts

[
2
]

Y.T. and J.K.1
are A.J.K.’s parents.  They met in New York City in 1998 when they were both
studying there.  At the time, Ms. Y.T. was on a foreign student visa from Japan.
Mr. J.K.1, originally from Poland, had been sponsored by family members to
study in the United States.

[
3
]

Ms. Y.T.
and Mr. J.K.1 began living together shortly after they started dating in
December 1998, and they initially lived with Mr. J.K.1’s mother in New York.
They married in July 1999, when Ms. Y.T. was pregnant.  A.J.K. was born on […],
2000.

[
4
]

The young
family left Mr. J.K.1’s mother’s home and moved to a co-operative apartment
(“co-op”) in New York around February 2000. Ms. Y.T.’s parents lent her more
than $100,000 US to buy the co-op.

[
5
]

The family
immigrated to Canada in June 2002.  In August 2002, they bought a home in the
Annex area of Toronto for $495,000.  There was no mortgage on the home.  Mr.
J.K.1 contributed about $100,000 to the purchase price, and the balance of the
funds came from the sale of the New York co-op, and moneys received from Ms.
Y.T.’s parents.

[
6
]

Since
arriving in Canada, Ms. Y.T. has stayed at home on a full-time basis to look
after A.J.K.. Mr. J.K.1 works as the activities director at a nursing home, and
currently earns approximately $39,000 per year.

[
7
]

The
parties separated on March 16, 2005, when Ms. Y.T. took A.J.K. and left the
matrimonial home.

The
New York
years: January 2000 - June
2002

[
8
]

When A.J.K.
was born, Mr. J.K.1 was going to school during the day and working in the
evenings, and Ms. Y.T. stayed home to look after her.  In March 2000, Ms. Y.T.
returned to school two evenings a week for two semesters.  Her classes were
from 5 to 10 p.m., with travel time to school being about 40 minutes.  On those
nights, Mr. J.K.1 looked after A.J.K..  In January 2001, Ms. Y.T. returned to
school during the day in order to maintain her immigration status. She attended
school from January 2001 until June 2002 for three days a week.  On those days,
Ms. Y.T. took A.J.K. to daycare.  Ms. Y.T.’s evidence was that Mr. J.K.1 was
not home much during that period; however, Mr. J.K.1 submits that he was
actively and intimately involved in A.J.K.’s early years.  He says that he
helped care for her; bathed her; and that he took his family on outings in New
York.

The
Toronto
years: June 2002 – March
16, 2005, date of separation

[
9
]

Since
moving to Canada in June 2002, Ms. Y.T. has always stayed home with A.J.K..
Her evidence was that she has provided all the necessities for A.J.K.,
including feeding her; giving her baths; playing with her; reading to her;
taking her to the doctor and dentist; and taking her to her different
activities, including to the park, to the T.[…] program, which is a
pre-kindergarten English program, to the H.[…] Academy, and to public school.

[
10
]

According to Ms. Y.T., the marital
relationship deteriorated after the family moved to Canada. Mr. J.K.1 worked
during the day and attended school two or three nights a week. Her evidence was
that Mr. J.K.1 was always very critical of her and told her that she did not
know how to work in the home.  Whatever she did in the home, he would redo.  By
way of example, she stated that she would clean the house daily, but that it
was never good enough for Mr. J.K.1 who would then clean everything for a
second time.  Ms. Y.T. stated that she felt demeaned and humiliated.

[
11
]

In addition to the constant
criticism of her homemaking skills, Ms. Y.T. testified that Mr. J.K.1 became
obsessed with her former relationships, and that he would wake her up in the
middle of the night to discuss former boyfriends for hours. While Mr. J.K.1
denied that he had any extraordinary interest in Ms. Y.T.’s former
relationships, Ms. Y.T.’s evidence is supported by the facts that Mr. J.K.1
referred to her former relationships in his answer to the application, where
they have no relevance to the issues; Mr. J.K.1 asked Ms. Y.T.’s counsel in
five different letters to identify the man who accompanied Ms. Y.T. when she
dropped A.J.K. off for the first access visit; and Mr. J.K.1 admitted his
jealousy of her former boyfriends in a letter he wrote to her parents in
January 2005.  In this regard, Mr. J.K.1 suggested that the letter was not
translated properly, despite the translation being done by a certified
translator whom he had hired.

[
12
]

According to Ms. Y.T., Mr. J.K.1’s
behaviour towards her made her feel worthless, and after an argument in
September 2004, she told Mr. J.K.1 that she wanted a divorce.  A.Mr. K.
fluctuated between being very angry and begging her to stay in the marriage.  Ms.
Y.T. needed time to think and went to Japan with A.J.K. in early October 2004.
In fact, by that time, Ms. Y.T. had already traveled to Japan with A.J.K. 7
times, and the October 2004 trip was their 8th visit to Japan.

[
13
]

In mid-November 2004, a few weeks
after her return from Japan, Ms. Y.T. advised Mr. J.K.1 that she still wanted a
divorce. She testified that it was around this time that Mr. J.K.1 began to
take an interest in A.J.K.. In particular, there was evidence about an incident
involving A.J.K.’s schooling that seemed to accelerate the tension in the
relationship.

[
14
]

According to Ms. Y.T., in January
2005, she noticed that A.J.K. was experiencing some difficulties at her
English-speaking public school, H.[…] Public School, and missed her friends
from the H.[…] Academy, a Japanese school that she had previously attended. For
this reason, one afternoon Ms. Y.T. took A.J.K. back to the H.[…] Academy. Ms.
Y.T. stated that when Mr. J.K.1 discovered that A.J.K. had not been at H.[…]
Public School on that day, he became very angry.  Rather than telling Mr. J.K.1
the truth, Ms. Y.T. told Mr. J.K.1 that she had taken A.J.K. to the doctor.  Mr.
J.K.1 called the doctor to confirm what Ms. Y.T. told him, and when the lie was
revealed, Ms. Y.T. stated that Mr. J.K.1 became furious. She testified that he
made a number of phone calls to persons unknown wherein he stated that his wife
was abducting their child. Further, he hid a large knife, because he told her
that he did not know what he would do if he saw the knife.

[
15
]

On the other hand, Mr. J.K.1’s
evidence was that around this time, in early 2005, Ms. Y.T. repeatedly
threatened to take A.J.K. to Japan, and he became very concerned about what he
described as a possible abduction.  His concern prompted him to write a letter
to A.J.K.’s teacher at H.[…] Public School, stating, among other things, that
his wife had taken A.J.K. on a long stay in Japan without his knowledge, and
that his wife affirmed that she would abduct A.J.K. and he would not see her
again.  I note that had Mr. J.K.1 truly believed that Ms. Y.T. had taken A.J.K.
to Japan without his knowledge, he would have contacted the police or the
Japanese consulate, steps that he took later in March 2005, when she was still
living at home with him. Given all the evidence that I have heard, it is not
credible for Mr. J.K.1 to allege that Ms. Y.T. took A.J.K. out of the country
without his knowledge, and he did nothing about it, except to tell her teacher
after the fact. In any event, the letter triggered a meeting among Ms. Y.T. and
N.S., the school principal, and W.L., the school social worker, both of whom
gave evidence. Ms. N.S. recalled that Ms. Y.T. used the word ‘torture’ when
describing her situation. After hearing from Ms. Y.T., Ms. N.S. provided her
with the contact information for the Barbra Schlifer Commemorative Clinic (the
“Clinic”) in Toronto, a clinic for women who have been abused. This school
meeting was followed by a meeting among Ms. Y.T., Mr. J.K.1 and Mr. W.L..  Mr.
W.L.’s evidence was that Ms. Y.T. was very upset at the meeting, and he
suggested anger management counseling for Mr. J.K.1.

[
16
]

Ms. Y.T. met with a counselor from
the Clinic 2 or 3 times in February 2005. Ms. Y.T. also testified that in
February 2005, Mr. J.K.1 threatened to kill her “if she was not good”. Despite
not informing Mr. J.K.1 that she was attending the Clinic for counseling, he
became aware of her visits, and wrote to the Clinic on February 27, 2005, professing his love for his wife and daughter. Mr. J.K.1 also wrote to the Consul
General of Japan in early March 2005 because of his concern that Ms. Y.T. would
take A.J.K. to Japan.

[
17
]

Ms. Y.T. and A.J.K. left their
home on March 16, 2005. Ms. Y.T. did not tell Mr. J.K.1 she was leaving;
however, on that same day, Mr. J.K.1 received a fax from Ms. Y.T.’s counsel
advising that she and A.J.K. were safe and in Toronto. Ms. Y.T. served her
application for divorce and other relief on March 18, 2005.

After separation:  March 16, 2005 to date

[
18
]

On April 7, 2005, Ms. Y.T. was
granted temporary custody of A.J.K., and Mr. J.K.1 was granted Saturday access
from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.  The April 7
th
order also provided for child
support, a mutual restraining order, and permission for Mr. J.K.1 to do a
DNA/Paternity test.

[
19
]

On consent, on June 22, 2005, Saturday access was extended to 8 p.m. and Mr. J.K.1 was granted access on Wednesdays
from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m.  At that time, the Office of the Children’s Lawyer was
asked to investigate and report on whether A.J.K. had sufficient English
language skills to stay with Mr. J.K.1 on an overnight basis.

[
20
]

On August 23, 2005, the court ordered, among other things, that the existing custody arrangement should
continue; that A.J.K. be enrolled in a public school near where she lives, to
be agreed upon by the parents; that access be extended, to be overnight from
Friday to Saturday, and on Mondays from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m., as well as Wednesdays
from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m.; that there be telephone access on Tuesdays and
Thursdays; that the parties communicate about A.J.K. through a communication
book; that Ms. Y.T. be prohibited from moving A.J.K. out of the jurisdiction
without permission; and that Ms. Y.T. be prohibited from registering A.J.K.’s
family name in any name other than K..

Access visits

[
21
]

The access visits have been
without incident. While it appears that there may have been some tears from A.J.K.
in the initial moments of the early visits, by all accounts, A.J.K. enjoys the
time with her father.  Dr. Keith Sharp, an actuary, and Dr. Lucia Bertelli, a
PhD in the pharmacology field, are husband and wife and friends of Mr. J.K.1.
They have a daughter who is A.J.K.’s age, and they attended on numerous access
visits with Mr. J.K.1. They offered glowing accounts of Mr. J.K.1’s parenting
and the visits themselves. The access visits have also been documented by Mr.
J.K.1 with unusual detail.

[
22
]

In particular, Mr. J.K.1 has kept
a written and photographic record of each visit. On average, he has described
each of some 60 access visits in 2-3 pages of single-spaced, typed or
handwritten notes. These 120 -180 pages of notes describe everything about the
visits, including what he and A.J.K. did; with whom they spent time, as they
were almost always with other people for at least some part of the visit; what A.J.K.
told him; what A.J.K. was wearing, and what she ate. In addition, the notes,
which are sometimes addressed directly to A.J.K., regularly express Mr. J.K.1’s
feelings about A.J.K. with passion and intensity. For example, in a July 2005
entry, Mr. J.K.1 wrote that he could not wait until Saturday, the access day,
when he could kiss and hug A.J.K. again, smell her hair, feel her hand; they could
run with each other again and look into each other’s eyes. Describing an August
10, 2005 visit, Mr. J.K.1 wrote that he had to hold back his tears and that he
did not need anything but to be with A.J.K.. In another August entry written
directly to A.J.K., Mr. J.K.1 stated that he missed her so much he could not
stop thinking of her, and that he could not hold back his tears when she had
telephoned him the previous day. Another journal entry states that Mr. J.K.1
had decided to devote his life to A.J.K., and expresses the hope that he and A.J.K.
can survive the difficult time in their lives until January 2006. A November
2005 entry states that he was thinking of A.J.K. every minute of the day, and
although she was sick that day, he hoped that she was looking at “their star”
out of the window. Other excerpts from the entries include Mr. J.K.1 stating
that A.J.K. is the reason for his life; that he loves her more than life
itself; that when he is alone, he feels shy, but that all that changes when he
is with A.J.K.; that he is not just A.J.K.’s father, but her friend, and that
she is his best friend. He describes his heart pounding when he is going to see
A.J.K., and writes about an almost fatherly hunger for her touch.  In a
September 2005 entry, Mr. J.K.1 compared leaving A.J.K. at the end of a visit
to the Africans brought to slavery, to Jewish families in World War II, and to
families in Sudan. Ms. Y.T. was not aware of the contents of these access
journals until the cross-examination of Mr. J.K.1 at trial.

Parenting plans

Mother

[
23
]

Ms. Y.T. submitted a parenting
plan at the start of the trial. The plan proposes that A.J.K. will live with
her in Japan on a permanent basis. Initially, mother and daughter will live
with Ms. Y.T.’s parents.  If and when they move from the grandparents’ home, Ms.
Y.T. intends to live close by, so that her parents can assist with taking care
of A.J.K. after school.  The access provisions of the original parenting plan
that Ms. Y.T. proposed are summarized as follows:

Two weeks in Toronto every summer.  Ms. Y.T.
proposed that she would  travel to Canada with A.J.K. every summer, at her
expense. She proposed daily access initially for the first two days, and
overnight access at Mr. J.K.1's home for the rest of the two-week period, provided
that A.J.K. is comfortable with the arrangements;

Once A.J.K. is 13 years old, she would travel on her
own to Canada for up to 3 weeks each summer;

Three-weeks of access in Japan each year. Again, Ms.
Y.T. proposed daily access initially for the first two days and overnight
access for the rest of the three-week period, provided that A.J.K. is
comfortable with the arrangements.

Weekly telephone calls from A.J.K. to Mr. J.K.1;
daily calls from Mr. J.K.1 to A.J.K.; internet access and email communication
when A.J.K. can read and write; and a web camera to enhance communication.

[
24
]

The parenting plan also included Ms.
Y.T.’s school plans for A.J.K. and provisions for enhancing A.J.K.'s English
skills.

[
25
]

However, after the detailed
journal entries of Mr. J.K.1’s access visits were disclosed on
cross-examination, Ms. Y.T. amended her parenting plan.    The access in the
revised plan is 2-weeks of access, once per year, alternating between Japan and
Canada.  One year Ms. Y.T. will come to Canada at her expense; the following
year Mr. J.K.1 will travel to Japan at his expense. This access would be daily,
with no overnight arrangements.  The revised parenting plan provides that Ms.
Y.T. shall have the discretion to terminate access if she determines that it is
having a negative psychological or emotional impact on A.J.K.. There is
provision for A.J.K. to call Mr. J.K.1 weekly, enhanced by a web camera.  Ms.
Y.T. wants to be able to monitor the calls. There is also provision for one
letter per week from Mr. J.K.1, with Ms. Y.T. having the right to review the
contents, and email access to Ms. Y.T. only for the purpose of scheduling the
annual access visits. Ms. Y.T. also proposed to send photographs and translated
report cards to Mr. J.K.1 and to keep Mr. J.K.1 informed about A.J.K.’s health.
The changes to access were made because of Ms. Y.T.’s concern for A.J.K.’s
emotional, psychological, and physical well-being after learning of the content
of the journal entries. More specifically, in cross-examination, Ms. Y.T. stated,
with some obvious reluctance, that the journal entries caused her to have a
concern that A.J.K. would be sexually assaulted by Mr. J.K.1.

Father

[
26
]

Mr. J.K.1’s parenting plan
proposed that A.J.K. remain in the same school she currently attends, and that A.J.K.
be enrolled in the school’s morning and afternoon daycare when he is at work.
He has rented an apartment close to the school and intends to move in late
January 2006. He proposed a shared residency arrangement, with A.J.K. spending
alternate weeks in each parent’s home. His plan indicated that his mother is
willing to relocate from New York to Toronto to assist in the transitional
period of A.J.K.’s life, although there was no evidence on this point.  His
plan also includes detailed future educational plans for A.J.K.; a provision
that she will be raised Catholic; and a detailed holiday-sharing schedule. Mr.
J.K.1’s parenting plan attempts to ensure that both parents will be involved in
making decisions about A.J.K.’s well-being.

Custody

[
27
]

This is an original application,
and accordingly, the first issue to be decided is custody (
Bjornson v.
Creighton
(2002),
2002 CanLII 45125 (ON CA)
, 62 O.R. (3d) 236 (C.A.)). At this time, as there are no
grounds for granting a divorce, the custody determination is governed by
s. 24

of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12 (the “Act”).

[
28
]

Subsection 24(1)
of the
Act
sets
out the principle that custody decisions shall be determined on the basis of
the best interests of the child.
Subsection 24(2)
outlines the factors that a
court should consider together with all the needs and circumstances of the
child.

[
29
]

Subsection 24(2)(a) provides that
the court shall consider

(a)        the love, affection and emotional ties
between the child and,

(i)

each person entitled to or claiming custody of or access to the child,

(ii)

other members of the child’s family who reside with the child, and

(iii)

persons involved in the care and upbringing of the child.

[
30
]

I am satisfied that A.J.K. enjoys
the love of both parents; however, I am also of the view that it is Ms. Y.T.
who has most consistently and regularly cared for A.J.K..  In the early years
in New York, Mr. J.K.1 only cared for A.J.K. while Ms. Y.T. was at school 2
evenings per week.  Indeed, given his own evidence that in the first year of
the marriage, he both worked full-time and attended school, and that in the
second year he worked at two jobs for some 70-75 hours a week, it is not
reasonable to accept that Mr. J.K.1 had much more time or energy left for A.J.K..
Once the family moved to Toronto, Ms. Y.T. stayed home and cared for A.J.K..
Again, at periods in Toronto, Mr. J.K.1 was working full-time and attending
school, which naturally limited his ability to attend to A.J.K.’s daily needs.

[
31
]

I have also considered A.J.K.'s
English-speaking ability in concluding that it has been Ms. Y.T. who has had
the primary care for A.J.K., and who has the more substantial connection to A.J.K..
A.J.K.’s first language is Japanese. Indeed, the evidence supports Ms. Y.T.’s
testimony that A.J.K. spoke little English when she and Mr. J.K.1 separated.
This evidence includes the evidence of Mr. D.T., a friend of the family, who
gave evidence on behalf of Mr. J.K.1.  Mr. D.T. wrote a letter in support of Mr.
J.K.1 that stated that A.J.K. spoke little English at the age of three, and
showed little improvement in the following two years. I have also considered
the report from Liana Lowenstein, a clinical investigator with the Office of
the Children’s Lawyer, dated November 6, 2005 and written after 2 visits with A.J.K.
and Ms. Y.T., and 2 visits with A.J.K. and Mr. J.K.1.  The report indicates
that A.J.K.'s English is limited, although she could communicate to some extent
and sufficiently well to express her needs when in the care of Mr. J.K.1. These
visits by Ms. Lowenstein occurred in August and September 2005, when A.J.K. was
already enjoying regular access with her father, and being exposed to more
English. While Mr. J.K.1 suggests that A.J.K. did not speak much English when
she was with Ms. Lowenstein because Ms. Y.T. told her not to speak, I do not
accept this submission, given that Mr. J.K.1’s own letter to Ms. T., a teacher
at H.[…] Public School, dated January 25, 2005, stated that A.J.K. does not
speak the English language and that he cannot communicate with her. In my view,
the fact that A.J.K. spoke little English by early 2005 and there was reason to
investigate her ability to communicate with Mr. J.K.1 on access visits suggests
that Mr. J.K.1 has overstated his involvement with her prior to that time.

[
32
]

I have also considered the love,
affection, and emotional ties between A.J.K. and other members of her family.
As stated, A.J.K. has traveled to Japan with her mother 8 times.   Each visit
took place at Ms. Y.T.’s parents’ home, where she stayed for 3-5 weeks.  On
those visits, A.J.K.  would also spend time with her cousins in Japan, the
children of Ms. Y.T.’s brother. Mrs. M.T., A.J.K.’s grandmother, traveled from Japan
for the trial. She testified that in addition to A.J.K. visiting her in Japan,
she visited A.J.K. once in New York and once in Toronto, and that they speak on
the telephone.  I am satisfied she and A.J.K. have a close relationship.

[
33
]

Ms. Y.T.’s parents have also been
financially generous to their daughter and granddaughter.  In addition to the
cash provided for the co-op apartment in New York and the home in Toronto, they
paid for A.J.K.’s day care in New York, her tuition fees for schooling, and
they have bought her clothing and shoes. While these are material items only,
they are further indicia of the special relationship that has been established
by the frequent visits and regular contact.

[
34
]

While Mr. J.K.1’s brother J.K.2
and sister B.P., A.J.K.’s godparents, traveled by overnight bus to attend the
trial, the evidence does not support Mr. J.K.1's submissions that they too have
established relationships with A.J.K.. Mr. J.K.2 was unable to provide any
reliable evidence about how often he may have visited A.J.K. when she was in New
York, although he did concede that it was not that often, since his brother
was working a great deal and he did not visit when his brother was not at home.
In the same way, he could not quantify the number of times, even approximately,
that he had visited the family in Toronto. According to Ms. Y.T., he came to Toronto
once to visit, and stayed for about a week. Similarly, while Ms. B.P. testified
that she lived at her mother’s home along with Mr. J.K.1 and his family, and
often babysat A.J.K. so that Mr. J.K.1 could go out with Ms. Y.T., Ms. B.P.
acknowledged that she arrived in New York on around January 27 or 28, 2000, and
that her brother and his family moved to their own home in February 2000.   In
addition, Ms. B.P. did not come to Toronto at any time before Ms. Y.T. and Mr.
J.K.1 separated in March 2005. Ms. Y.T. testified that Mr. J.K.1’s mother came
to Toronto twice, once in November 2004, and once in January 2005, and that
both times she stayed for 3 days.

[
35
]

With respect to
subsection
24(2)
(b) of the
Act
, at age 6 A.J.K. is still too young to ascertain any
meaningful views or preferences of her own.

[
36
]

Subsection 24(2)
(c) of the
Act

addresses the length of time the child has lived in a stable home environment.
In this regard, I note that Mr. J.K.1 is critical of Ms. Y.T. for, among other
things, moving with A.J.K. to a new neighbourhood in March 2005. However, I
accept Ms. Y.T.’s evidence that she felt afraid of Mr. J.K.1, and that he made
her feel worthless. It is precisely these difficulties that forced Ms. Y.T. to
leave the matrimonial home that had been purchased largely with funds from her
family, and move to a 2-bedroom apartment in a new neighbourhood. Despite the
move, which was, no doubt, disruptive to A.J.K. as it was to Ms. Y.T., Ms. Y.T.
has been a stable parent for A.J.K. since birth.

[
37
]

Subsection 24(2)
(d) of the
Act

requires me to consider the ability and willingness of each person applying for
custody of the child to provide the child with guidance and education, the
necessaries of life and any special needs of the child.  In this case, the
evidence is that both parents are able to provide A.J.K. with guidance,
education, and the necessaries of life. I do not accept Mr. J.K.1’s suggestion
that Ms. Y.T. did not have A.J.K.’s best interests at heart when she made
arrangements for A.J.K. to attend the H.[…] Academy in January 2005. Ms. Y.T.
took A.J.K. to the H.[…] Academy because she was having some difficulty
adjusting to H.[…] Public School.  A.J.K. attended the Japanese school three
times in January 2005, thereby missing three afternoons of junior kindergarten
at H.[…] Public School. In my view, Ms. Y.T.’s attention to A.J.K.’s needs, and
the steps she has taken to ensure that her early school experience is a
positive one, demonstrate that Ms. Y.T. is motivated by A.J.K.’s best
interests.

[
38
]

There are, however, elements of Mr.
J.K.1’s parenting during access that suggest that in his desire to be attentive
to A.J.K., he accommodates her every request. For example, Mr. J.K.1 testified
that he always carries A.J.K. on his back, his shoulders or in his arms, the
only exception being when A.J.K. is playing with her own friends.  He indicated
that he never says “no” to A.J.K. when she wants to be carried on his back.
His journals describe them as being “glued together”. By way of further
example, in his journal entry of August 4, 2005, Mr. J.K.1 wrote: “When I am
alone, I feel shy.  Everything changes when A.J.K. is with me.  I am happy and
playful.  I feel like a child myself.  I am not only A.J.K.’s father…I am also
her friend.  There is no barrier between us. A.J.K. speaks to me like to her
friends and I do the same.” In subsequent journal entries he repeats that A.J.K.
is his best friend or true friend. A.J.K. is a healthy 6 year old. A parent’s
responsibility is to establish age appropriate boundaries for children and to
help them become independent in age appropriate ways.  In my view, Mr. J.K.1’s
practices of always carrying his daughter, always acceding to her requests to
be carried, and aspiring to be her friend, do not offer the best guidance for A.J.K..
In addition, there was evidence from both Ms. Y.T. and Mr. J.K.1 that on A.J.K.’s
first access visit on April 9, 2005, Mr. J.K.1 was on the floor of the subway
platform, sobbing when he left A.J.K..  Whether the sobbing was for 15 minutes,
as alleged by Ms. Y.T., or 15 seconds, as alleged by Mr. J.K.1, this kind of
demonstration would not be helpful to A.J.K. at what was clearly a difficult
moment.

[
39
]

Subsection 24(2)
(e) of the
Act

requires an examination of the proposed parenting plans for the child.  In my
view, while both plans provide for A.J.K.’s well-being and include exposure to
English and Japanese, there are also problems with both plans.  In Ms. Y.T.’s
revised parenting plan, the access between Mr. J.K.1 and A.J.K. is
significantly reduced from that which was presented in her original plan.  As
stated, the amendments were made after the existence and content of Mr. J.K.1’s
journals were revealed during cross-examination.  Ms. Y.T. is concerned about
the copious journal entries, as she feels they suggest an inappropriate focus
on A.J.K., and are often written in language that is typically used in a
romantic relationship.  I am skeptical about Mr. J.K.1’s explanation that the
language he used was a result of English not being his first language.
Throughout the trial and in the written material, there has been no indication
that Mr. J.K.1 struggles with English, or that he does not appreciate the
nuances of the English language.  Nonetheless, there has also been no evidence
that there have been any problems with the access that has been in place for
some 10 months, or that A.J.K. does not enjoy access.  There is also no
evidence that the nature of the journals will lead to the problems for A.J.K.
that Ms. Y.T. fears.  Then again, Mr. J.K.1’s proposal includes a provision
that the parents attend counseling together to improve their communication and
parenting skills and that they consult each other regularly about important
issues in A.J.K.’s life.  These suggestions completely disregard Ms. Y.T.’s
evidence that she is unable to communicate with Mr. J.K.1 because she is afraid
of him, and finds him controlling and obsessive. As stated in
Kaplanis v.
Kaplanis
,
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, [2005] O.J. No. 275 (C.A.), a decision of the Ontario Court of
Appeal in the context of a joint custody order, there must be some evidence
before the court that, despite their differences, the parents are able to
communicate effectively with each other. In this case, as the only way that the
parents can communicate is with a written communication book, Mr. J.K.1’s
proposal for frequent consultation between both parents will simply not be
workable.

[
40
]

Subsection 24(2)
(f) of the
Act

directs a consideration of the permanence and stability of the family unit with
whom it is proposed that the child will live. Historically, Ms. Y.T. has provided
permanence and stability to A.J.K.. Except for the access visits, A.J.K. has
not been away from her care for even one night. A.J.K. has also spent extended
periods in her young life with her maternal grandparents in Japan, and I am
satisfied on all the evidence, including that of Mr. Toro Sasaki, a witness
called by Mr. J.K.1, that A.J.K. can communicate easily in Japanese. While I
accept that A.J.K. enjoys her time with her father, I am not persuaded that she
has as strong a relationship with her other paternal relatives as she does with
her extended maternal family.

[
41
]

With respect to
subsection 24(2)
(g) of the
Act
, both
parents have an equal relationship by blood to A.J.K., and as such, this factor
is neutral.

[
42
]

I have
also considered the maximum contact principle that a child shall have as much
contact with each parent as is in the best interests of the child, as
articulated in
subsection 16(10)
of the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3
(2
nd
Supp.), notwithstanding that this is a custody determination
under the
Children’s Law Reform Act
(
see
Woodhouse v. Woodhouse

(1996),
1996 CanLII 902 (ON CA)
,
29 O.R. (3d) 417 (C.A
.)).

[
43
]

In sum, for the foregoing reasons,
I am satisfied that Ms. Y.T. is and has always been the primary caregiver for A.J.K.,
and that A.J.K. is by all accounts, a happy, healthy, and outgoing child.   I
am of the view that it is in the best interests of A.J.K. to be in the sole
custody of her mother, Y.T., with access to her father, J.K.1.

Mobility

[
44
]

Ms. Y.T. has requested that she be
allowed to move to Japan with A.J.K.. Therefore, I now turn to the second stage
of the inquiry set out in
Gordon v. Goertz
,
1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 (S.C.C.)
and the factors the court must consider when one parent wants to move the
residence of the child to a location that is far from the other parent (see
also
Bjornson
, supra
).

[
45
]

Paragraph 49 of
Gordon v.
Goertz
summarizes the relevant principles on questions of mobility.  It
provides as follows:

…

4.  The inquiry does not begin with a legal
presumption in favour of the custodial parent, although the custodial parent’s
views are entitled to great respect.

5.  Each case turns on its own unique
circumstances.  The only issue is the best interest of the child in the
particular circumstances of the case.

6.  The focus is on the best interests of the child,
not the interests and rights of the parents.

7.  More particularly the judge should consider,
inter alia:

(a)        the
existing custody arrangement and relationship between the child and the
custodial parent;

(b)        the
existing access arrangement and the relationship between the child and the
access parent;

(c)        the desirability of
maximizing contact between the child and both parents;

(d)        the views of the child;

(e)        the
custodial parent’s reason for moving, only in the exceptional case where it is
relevant to that parent’s ability to meet the needs of the child;

(f)         disruption to the
child of a change in custody;

(g)        disruption
to the child consequent on removal from family, schools, and the community he
or she has come to know.

[
46
]

As the governing question is what
is in the best interests of the child, much of the evidence that was considered
in the review of the custody question will also be germane in this analysis.

[
47
]

I begin with point 4 of the
principles set out in
Gordon v. Goertz
. In light of my preceding
analysis, Ms. Y.T. is the custodial parent, and her views are entitled to great
respect.  I am satisfied that Ms. Y.T. sincerely and passionately believes that
in light of the already established relationship that A.J.K. has with her
maternal grandparents, her facility in Japanese, and the emotional and
financial stability that living in Japan will offer, it is in A.J.K.’s best
interests that she be allowed to move to Japan.

[
48
]

I also note that point 6 of the
Gordan
v. Goertz
principles reiterates that the focus should be on the best
interests of the child, and not the interests and rights of the parents.
Throughout his evidence and written material, Mr. J.K.1 often focused on his
rights or needs as A.J.K.’s father, at times paying only lip service to A.J.K.’s
best interests. In this regard, I note Mr. J.K.1’s own personal history.  He
grew up in Poland and was raised by only his father from the time he was about
11 or 12 years old until he moved to the United States when he was 20.  During
these years, he never saw his mother, although they did speak on the telephone,
she sent him gifts, and they exchanged correspondence.  Despite admitting that
he grew up in a loving home and that he had a positive childhood even without
the physical presence of his mother, Mr. J.K.1 refused to acknowledge that Ms.
Y.T.’s original parenting plan, where he would have 5 weeks of access plus
other contact, was reasonable.  It is logical to draw the inference from this
stance that Mr. J.K.1 was thinking of his own needs as much, if not more, than
he was thinking of A.J.K.’s needs.

[
49
]

I have already reviewed the
existing custody arrangement and relationship between A.J.K. and Ms. Y.T..  I
am satisfied that the relationship is a positive and close one, and that A.J.K.
is thriving under her mother’s care.

[
50
]

Similarly, I have already
reviewed the existing access arrangement and the relationship between Mr. J.K.1
and A.J.K..  As stated, the evidence is that the access visits have proceeded
in a positive way.  It is clear that Mr. J.K.1 makes every effort to plan days
for A.J.K. that are busy and fun-filled.

[
51
]

The desirability of maximizing
contact between the child and both parents, point 7(c) of the
Gordon v.
Goertz
considerations, is a mandatory principle under the
Divorce Act
,
but it is not absolute. I am satisfied that there is no evidence to support Ms.
Y.T.’s apprehension that the journal entries prove a possibility of any sexual
misconduct by Mr. J.K.1 against A.J.K., or other detrimental conduct by him
toward her.  Nonetheless, the entries do certainly suggest a fixation on A.J.K.
that could be considered obsessive. In my view, in this case, this  tempers the
principle that maximizing the contact with Mr. J.K.1 is necessarily in A.J.K.’s
best interests.  (See
Young v. Young,

1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3 (S.C.C.))

[
52
]

With respect to point 7(d) of
Gordon
v. Goertz
, as A.J.K. has just turned 6, her views are not reliably
ascertainable.

[
53
]

Point 7(e) of
Gordon v. Goertz

directs the court to consider the custodial parent’s reasons for moving, only
in the exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent’s ability to meet
the needs of the child.  In my view, this is one of those cases.   Ms. Y.T. has
no family or close friends in Canada.  She has testified about her relationship
with Mr. J.K.1, and how she is unable to deal with what she describes as his
obsessive and controlling personality.  As already noted, her evidence was that
he intimidated her and made her feel worthless. I am satisfied by reason of
counsel’s letter dated October 14, 2005 that Mr. J.K.1 did threaten to contact
the Children’s Aid Society, despite there being no evidence of improper
parenting by Ms. Y.T..  Indeed, it was the evidence of W.L., the school social
worker, that there were no protection concerns relating to Ms. Y.T.. I also
note the numerous groundless allegations in Mr. J.K.1’s reply to Ms. Y.T.’s
application and conclude that Ms. Y.T.’s feelings are not unsubstantiated.  It
was clear to me from the manner in which Ms. Y.T. gave her evidence, without
ever looking directly at Mr. J.K.1, that she is frightened of him. In addition,
it is likely that if she remains in Toronto, Ms. Y.T.'s English skills will
always be some impediment to employment, whereas they will be an asset to
employment in Japan. She testified that if she is required to remain in Toronto,
she will study to be a dog groomer, whereas she has provided evidence of a job
offer in Japan where she will earn $42,000 annually.  After a difficult
relationship with Mr. J.K.1, Ms. Y.T. seeks the security and emotional support
that being with her family in Japan will provide, and the financial
independence that employment will offer.  It is logical to infer that while a
very good parent now, Ms. Y.T. will be an even better parent when she regains
her confidence, self esteem, and emotional stability, and can be financially
independent (see
Bjornson
, supra
and
Sheikh v. Sheikh
,
2005 CanLII 14151 (ON SC)
, [2005]
O.J. No. 1712 (Sup. Ct. J.)).  This will happen much more readily in Japan than
in Toronto.

[
54
]

Points 7(f) and (g) of the
Gordon
v. Goertz

principles address the disruption to the child of a change in
custody and the disruption consequent on removal from family, school and the
community he or she has come to know.  As Ms. Y.T. has testified that she will
not move to Japan if she is not permitted to take A.J.K. with her, there will
be no disruption from a change in custody.  I recognize that a move to Japan
will disrupt the pattern of the relationship that has developed in the last 10
months or so between A.J.K. and her father, and that there will be fewer
opportunities for exposure to her Polish heritage in Japan.  I also recognize
the importance of these concerns; however, they must be measured against other
factors.  As indicated, I am satisfied that A.J.K. has a stronger relationship
with her extended family in Japan than she has with her extended family in New
York, despite the difference in proximity. A.J.K. has only lived in Toronto
for 3 ½ years, and within this short period, she has lived in two different
neighbourhoods.  She is only 6 years old, and is about to start senior
kindergarten. While the evidence has been that A.J.K. has a number of young
friends, given her age, these are not yet significant relationships. This case
can be distinguished from
Bartlett v. Bartlett
,
2004 ONCJ 276 (CanLII)
, [2004] O.J. No. 4659
(OCJ) cited by Mr. J.K.1, where the children had gone to the same school, lived
in the same neighbourhood, and had established relationships with friends,
neighbours, and relatives for a number of years in Canada. In addition, in
Bartlett
,
the children did not speak Japanese. On the contrary, Ms. Y.T. has already been
able to register A.J.K. as a Japanese citizen by virtue of her own citizenship.
A.J.K. speaks Japanese.  When the totality of A.J.K.’s visits to Japan is
considered, A.J.K. has already spent about 6 months in Japan.

[
55
]

I have also considered Mr. J.K.1’s
concern that A.J.K. will face discrimination in Japan because of her mixed
heritage (see
Convention on the Rights of the Child,
1989 G.A. Res.44/25
28 I.L.M. 1456, cited by Mr. J.K.1).  Firstly, I note that there was no
reliable connection between the material Mr. J.K.1 relied upon and the area in Japan
where A.J.K. will be living. In addition, it was Ms. Y.T.’s view that this
discrimination would not be a problem in the current Japan, and that, in any
event, A.J.K. looks Japanese. In my view, given Ms. Y.T.’s devotion to A.J.K.,
she will be attentive to and properly deal with any racism toward A.J.K. in Japan,
just as she would do if A.J.K. faced a similar problem in Canada.

[
56
]

In my view, it is in A.J.K.’s best
interests that she be permitted to re-locate with her mother to Japan. Mobility
cases are always very difficult. As was stated by the Court of Appeal in
Singer
v. Davila-Singer
,
[2003] O.J. No. 3231 (C.A.)
, “ Sadly, there can be no
judicial resolution of this issue before us that will avoid profound
disappointment to one of these caring parents or completely avoid the risk of
harm to the interests of the children.” The reality is that a move to Japan
will reduce the amount of time that A.J.K. and her father spend together, at
least until she is much older. However, that being said, it does not follow
that the move to Japan will not be in A.J.K.’s best interests (see
Bjornson
,
supra
). When all the facts of this family situation are measured against
the factors enunciated by McLachlin J. in
Gordon v. Goertz
, I am
satisfied that the best interests of A.J.K. will be met by the move to Japan as
proposed by Ms. Y.T..  In his testimony, Mr. J.K.1 acknowledged that despite
not even seeing his mother for at least 8 years, they were able to maintain a
loving relationship, and he had a positive childhood.  I sincerely hope that Mr.
J.K.1 can appreciate this, accept this decision and do his best to facilitate
the transition for A.J.K..

Access

[
57
]

I am not persuaded that the nature
of the access proposed in Ms. Y.T.’s original parenting plan is inappropriate. Ms.
Y.T. amended the parenting plan after learning of the journals; however, as I
have indicated, there is no evidence that satisfies me that the journals show a
need to limit access. Despite the hyperbole and somewhat excessive expression
of devotion in the journals, I am satisfied that Mr. J.K.1 loves A.J.K. and
that she loves her father.  Details of access once Ms. Y.T. moves to Japan are
set out in paragraph 64.

Security

[
58
]

I recognize Mr. J.K.1’s concern
that Japan is not a signatory to the Hague Convention, and Mr. J.K.1 would have
no means of enforcing a Canadian order in Japan. Indeed, in her original
parenting plan, Ms. Y.T. proposed to post a $50,000 bond to address this
concern, but she withdrew the proposal when she submitted a revised access plan
after the journals had been revealed. There appear to be a number of reasons
for this change to her proposal.  Firstly, in light of Ms. Y.T.’s financial
circumstances, including the expenses of the trial, she submits that it is no
longer appropriate. Secondly, Ms. Y.T. submits that the evidence at trial
demonstrates that Ms. Y.T. is a credible person, and will abide by all court
orders.  Finally, Ms. Y.T. submits that given the extent to which access and
all minutiae regarding A.J.K. have been  monitored and recorded by Mr. J.K.1, a
bond would be used by Mr. J.K.1 to harass Ms. Y.T. in the event of any
circumstance at all that he could argue to be a breach of my order.

[
59
]

All the evidence indicates that Ms.
Y.T. would abide by a Canadian court order.  I note, for instance, that when
she went to Japan with A.J.K. after a serious argument with Mr. J.K.1 in the
fall of 2004, Ms. Y.T.’s evidence was that she returned to Canada with A.J.K.
after being advised by lawyers in Japan that any family litigation must proceed
in Canada. In addition, immediately after she left the matrimonial home on
March 16, 2005, Ms. Y.T. had her counsel advise Mr. J.K.1 that she and A.J.K.
were in Toronto and safe. She has complied fully with all access orders.

[
60
]

Just as there is no evidence to
suggest that Ms. Y.T. would not respect an order of this court, there is also
no evidence to suggest that a bond, if ordered, would be used by Mr. J.K.1 to
harass Ms. Y.T..  While it appears that Mr. J.K.1 has written voluminous
correspondence to Ms. Y.T.’s counsel, this does not lead to the conclusion that
he would exploit or misuse the bond. Mr. J.K.1, while advocating passionately
for custody, has not brought any improper motions or abused the court process
since the date of separation. The simple fact is that with my order, Ms. Y.T.
will be able to relocate to a jurisdiction thousands of miles from Canada. A
substantial security bond was included in Ms. Y.T.’s original proposed custody
and access plan.  I find nothing has changed since that time, except that Ms.
Y.T. has, in fact, borne the cost of the trial. Accordingly, out of an
abundance of caution, I am satisfied that it is reasonable and appropriate for Ms.
Y.T. to post a security bond in the amount of $20,000 to secure her compliance
with the terms of this order.

Religion

[
61
]

Mr. J.K.1, in his parenting plan,
expresses his wish that A.J.K. be raised according to the Catholic religion.
In
Young v. Young
, supra
, the Court determined that the best interests
of the children is the governing consideration in questions relating to the
religious upbringing of children.  The court should not choose between the
parents’ religions.  Ms. Y.T., as the custodial parent, shall determine A.J.K.’s
religion, but Mr. J.K.1 shall have the right to share his religion with A.J.K.
during access visits. There is nothing before me to suggest that this would not
be in her best interests.

Change of Name

[
62
]

Ms. Y.T. requests an order
allowing A.J.K. to use “T.” as her legal surname in Japan and in any other
Japanese-related organizations. Under subsection 5(1)(b) of the
Ontario
Change
of Name Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.7, a person with lawful custody may apply to
the authority to change the child’s surname, unless a court order prohibits the
change. The right to change a child’s name is an incident of custody and any
dispute about a proposed name change is  decided according to the best
interests of the child.   Mr. J.K.1 objected to the above request.  He is
concerned that the change of name would break the substantial link that he has
to A.J.K. and he wants to continue to play an integral role in the development
of A.J.K..  I am concerned that Ms. Y.T.’s proposal may cause confusion with
different legal surnames for A.J.K. on her Canadian traveling documents and
other records, such as school and medical reports in Japan. Therefore, I
conclude that it is not in A.J.K.’s best interests to have her surname changed
on her Japanese documents.

Child support

[
63
]

Mr. J.K.1 earns $39,000 per year.
Mr. J.K.1 asks that there be no child support awarded.  It appears that Mr.
J.K.1’s objection is grounded in the expense of the access visits.  While
travel and accommodation in Japan is expensive, I have reviewed Mr. J.K.1’s
financial statement, and he has not satisfied me that any undue hardship,
specifically, an inability to visit A.J.K., will result if he pays child
support.  (
Section 10
of the
Child Support Guidelines
O.Reg.391/97 as
am.).  As well, the governing consideration continues to be the best interest
of A.J.K., and I am satisfied that child support is in her best interests.

Order

[
64
]

Accordingly, based on all of the
above, I order as follows:

1.

Ms.
Y.T. shall have sole custody of A.J.K., born […], 2000,  and she is permitted
to move to Japan with A.J.K. forthwith, upon compliance with paragraph 14 of
this order, so that A.J.K. can be enrolled in school in Japan as soon as
possible.

2.

All
of A.J.K.’s travel documents that have been deposited with the court shall be
returned to Ms. Y.T. immediately.  Mr. J.K.1 shall cooperate and sign any
documents or consents that may be required to have A.J.K. travel with her
mother to Japan.

3.

Mr.
J.K.1 shall  have access to A.J.K. as follows:

(a)

Two weeks in Toronto every summer.  Ms. Y.T. or another family member
shall travel to Canada with A.J.K. every summer, at Ms. Y.T.’s expense. Mr.
J.K.1 shall have daily access initially for the first week (from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.), and overnight access at Mr. J.K.1's home for the second week period.
Starting in 2008, the daily access shall be reduced to the first 3 days, with
overnight access at Mr. J.K.1’s home for the rest of the two-week period.

(b)

Once A.J.K. is 13 years old, Ms. Y.T. will send her on her own to Canada
for up to 3 weeks each summer for access with her father;

(c)

Three weeks of access in Japan each year, the expense to be paid by Mr.
J.K.1 and any of his extended family who wish to accompany him.  Mr. J.K.1 and
his extended family shall have daily access initially for the first three days
(from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.), and overnight access for the rest of the three-week
period. If requested by Mr. J.K.1 through email, Ms. Y.T. shall assist with
finding suitable accommodation for Mr. J.K.1 for these periods, and she shall
provide any such information by email.

(d)

Mr. J.K.1 and Ms. Y.T. shall agree to the access schedule on or before
March 15 each year.  Ms. Y.T. shall travel to Canada during the time A.J.K. is
on holidays from school.  In the event that Mr. J.K.1 has not advised Ms. Y.T.
of his intended access visits by March 15 of any year, either by email or
registered letter, Ms. Y.T. shall be free to make alternate plans for her and A.J.K..

(e)

Ms. Y.T. shall arrange for A.J.K. to telephone Mr. J.K.1 once a week. Mr.
J.K.1 shall be entitled to telephone A.J.K. twice per week, should he choose to
do so.

(f)

Ms. Y.T. shall provide internet access and email communication access to
A.J.K. to enable her to communicate with her father as soon as A.J.K. can read
and write in English.

(g)

A web camera shall be set up in Ms. Y.T.’s home within 30 days of her
arrival in Japan  to enhance communication between Mr. J.K.1 and A.J.K..

(h)

Such other access as agreed by the parties.

4.

Each
parent shall keep the other informed as to his or her current address and
telephone number and shall notify each other in writing at least sixty days
prior to any change in residence.

5.

Ms.
Y.T. shall advise Mr. J.K.1 of any major issues regarding A.J.K.’s health or
education.

6.

Mr.
J.K.1’s extended family (such as A.J.K.’s paternal grandparents and
godparents), if they wish, shall have telephone access to A.J.K. once per week;
days and times to be arranged with Ms. Y.T..  They shall also be entitled to
send gifts to A.J.K..

7.

Ms.
Y.T. shall take all necessary steps to maintain and improve A.J.K.'s English-language
skills so that she can continue to communicate in a meaningful way with her
father and her father’s extended family.

8.

Ms.
Y.T. shall maintain A.J.K.’s full current name as “A.J.K.” on all documents
relating to her citizenship and schooling in Japan, where it is possible to do
so, and shall take no steps to legally change her name.  Both parents shall
cooperate, including the signing of any documents that may be required to
effect this.

9.

Mr.
J.K.1 shall not harass Ms. Y.T..

10.

Mr. J.K.1 shall be
restrained from applying for any passport for A.J.K., without the written
consent of Ms. Y.T., or further court order.

11.

Commencing on March 1, 2006, and on the first day of each subsequent month, Mr. J.K.1 shall pay $317 per
month as child support, based on his income of $39,000 per year.

12.

Mr. J.K.1 shall notify Ms.
Y.T. in writing within 30 days of any change in income or employment,  together
with proof of such change.

13.

Mr. J.K.1 shall be permitted
to expose A.J.K. to her Polish heritage.

14.
